text: The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time
auditor_note: Factual errors and medium/attribution errors only. Interpretation not flagged. Sources: Wikipedia (novel and play articles), National Theatre education resources, LitCharts, SparkNotes, SaveMyExams Eduqas GCSE revision notes, StageAgent, GradeSaver, Shmoop, SuperSummary, Seneca Learning AQA notes (for cross-reference). CRITICAL CONTEXT: Eduqas GCSE teaches the Simon Stephens 2012 play-text, not the Haddon novel. The play uses Siobhan as co-narrator reading Christopher's book, has no chapter numbers (those are a novel-only structural device), and ends differently from the novel.

fact_base.primary_text: Simon Stephens's stage adaptation of Mark Haddon's novel, first performed National Theatre (Cottesloe) 2 August 2012, directed by Marianne Elliott. Tony Award Best Play and Olivier Award Best Play.
fact_base.structure: Two acts. 39 speaking parts performed by 16 actors. Christopher onstage throughout.
fact_base.siobhan_role_in_play: Co-narrator: reads aloud from Christopher's book throughout the play, giving the work a play-within-a-play structure. Also his teacher/mentor at school. Her narration is the main device for communicating Christopher's inner world to the audience.
fact_base.siobhan_role_in_novel: Christopher's teacher (and one-on-one support figure) at his special school — she has worked with him for eight years. She encourages him to write the book but does NOT narrate in the novel; Christopher is the sole first-person narrator in the novel.
fact_base.chapter_numbers: Prime-numbered chapters (2, 3, 5, 7, 11... up to 233) are a NOVEL structural device. The play-text uses scenes, not chapters. Calling lesson units 'Chapters 2-89', 'Chapters 97-157', 'Chapters 163-233' imports the novel's organisation into a play-text course.
fact_base.wellington_breed: Wellington is Mrs Shears's large black poodle (not a golden retriever — Sandy, the golden retriever puppy, is given to Christopher by Ed at the end as a trust-rebuilding gift).
fact_base.sandy_breed: Sandy is explicitly described as a golden retriever puppy given by Ed to Christopher near the end.
fact_base.christopher_age: 15 years old, attending a special school in Swindon.
key_characters: Roger Shears/Mr Shears (Mrs Shears's ex-husband; Judy's partner)
Wellington (Mrs Shears's poodle, killed at start)
Sandy (golden retriever puppy, gift at end)
fact_base.play_vs_novel_ending: Novel: Christopher makes a declarative statement — 'And I know I can do this because I went to London on my own, and because I solved the mystery of Who Killed Wellington? And I found my mother and I was brave and I wrote a book and that means I can do anything.' Play: Christopher asks Siobhan a question — 'Does that mean I can do anything Siobhan?' This is a significant tonal and structural difference (declaration vs question, certainty vs aspiration).
fact_base.a_level_maths_onstage: In the play, after the main action ends, Christopher re-enters and works through his favourite A-level maths problem for the audience, with theatrical staging (music, lights, lasers, confetti). This post-show scene is a distinctive feature of the play-text, not present in the novel (where the A-level exam and A* result are narrated in prose).
fact_base.metaphor_quote: Christopher's position on metaphors appears in Chapter 29 of the novel: 'The word metaphor means carrying something from one place to another... it is when you describe something by using a word for something that it isn't... I think it should be called a lie because a pig is not like a day and people do not have skeletons in their cupboards.' The specific example in L6 ('When I say the dog ran this is true. When you say the sky was crying this is a lie because the sky does not cry') is a paraphrase/variant, not the exact text.
fact_base.prime_numbers_quote: Confirmed: 'Prime numbers are what is left when you have taken all the patterns away.' Christopher also says: 'I think prime numbers are like life. They are very logical but you could never work out the rules, even if you spent all your time thinking about them.' Both are authentic.
fact_base.whitbread: Novel won the Whitbread Novel Award and overall Whitbread Book of the Year 2003. It was published simultaneously in adult and children's imprints — first book to achieve this. The play won the Olivier Award for Best Play and the Tony Award for Best Play. The lessons mention only the novel's Whitbread win and omit the play's awards.
fact_base.judy_letters_quote: Confirmed: 'I am not a very good mother, Christopher. Maybe if things had been different... maybe if you'd been different... but that is not your fault.' appears in the novel's letters and is reproduced in the play.
fact_base.final_chapter_quote_full: Novel Chapter 233 full verified ending: 'And I know I can do this because I went to London on my own, and because I solved the mystery of Who Killed Wellington? And I found my mother and I was brave and I wrote a book and that means I can do anything.'
fact_base.detective_genre_reference: Title references Holmes story 'The Adventure of Silver Blaze': 'the curious incident of the dog in the night-time' (the dog did nothing — that was the curious incident). Confirmed correct.

findings.location: Opening paragraph and throughout all 8 lessons
findings.claim: All 8 lessons are written as analysis of 'the novel' by Mark Haddon — e.g. 'The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time was published in 2003 and became an immediate bestseller'; 'Haddon presents Christopher as...'; analytical verbs consistently attribute craft choices to 'Haddon' rather than 'Stephens'.
findings.issue: CRITICAL SYSTEMIC ERROR. Eduqas GCSE (WJEC) teaches the Simon Stephens 2012 stage adaptation (playscript), NOT the Haddon novel. Students will be examined on the play-text. Writing 8 lessons that analyse 'the novel' and attribute all craft decisions to 'Haddon' teaches students the wrong primary text. In the exam, students who write about 'the novel' and reference 'Haddon' instead of 'Stephens' / 'the play' may lose AO2 marks for inaccurate analysis of form and attribution of technique. The entire unit needs to be reframed around the play-text, with Stephens credited as the playwright/adapter and play-specific techniques (ensemble staging, Siobhan's narrator role, projected maths sequences, theatrical devices) foregrounded.
findings.correction: Reframe all 8 lessons to be explicit that the studied text is Simon Stephens's play-text (2012), adapted from Haddon's novel. Where craft choices are analysed, attribute them to 'Stephens' (e.g. 'Stephens uses Siobhan as co-narrator...', 'Stephens adapts Haddon's first-person narrative by...', 'the playwright gives Christopher the ensemble cast as a chorus...'). Where context is given about the novel, clearly distinguish it from the play. Add acknowledgement of the Tony and Olivier wins alongside the Whitbread.
findings.source: Eduqas GCSE English Literature specification; WJEC/Eduqas revision resources (SaveMyExams, LearnlyAI, official WJEC teaching materials) all specify 'the playscript' by Simon Stephens.

findings.location: Lesson title and structural organisation of Lessons 2, 3, 4
findings.claim: Lessons 2, 3, 4 are organised by chapter numbers: 'Chapters 2-89', 'Chapters 97-157', 'Chapters 163-233'.
findings.issue: Chapter numbers (prime-numbered chapters 2, 3, 5, 7... up to 233) are a structural device of Haddon's novel. The Stephens play-text does not have chapters — it is structured in scenes and two acts. Organising lessons around chapter numbers teaches students a structural feature that belongs to the novel, not to the play they will be examined on. Students who write in an exam about 'chapters' in the Stephens play will demonstrate a medium error.
findings.correction: Reorganise these lessons around act/scene structure of the play, or around plot stages (Act 1: Wellington's death, investigation, discovery of letters; Act 2: journey to London, reunion with Judy, return to Swindon, A-level exam). Acknowledge that the prime-numbered chapter structure is a NOVEL device that Stephens had to adapt — useful context but should be taught as 'how the novel is structured' not 'how the text is structured'.
findings.source: Wikipedia (play article): the play has two acts and uses scenes, not chapters. The chapter numbering is a well-documented feature of Haddon's novel.

findings.claim: "Siobhan is Christopher's teaching assistant at his special school — and the person who encourages him to write his book."
findings.issue: Two errors. (1) Siobhan's role: she is Christopher's teacher (and educational support figure), not merely a 'teaching assistant'. Sources including LitCharts, SparkNotes, National Theatre education materials all describe her as his teacher. The 'teaching assistant' label is a demotion of her role. (2) Most critically for Eduqas: the lesson does not describe Siobhan's defining role in the PLAY — that she is the co-narrator who reads aloud from Christopher's book throughout the performance. In the play, Siobhan's narrator function is arguably the most important theatrical device, transforming a first-person novel into a play-within-a-play. This play-specific role is absent from the character analysis.
findings.correction: Describe Siobhan as Christopher's teacher (not teaching assistant). Add the play-specific information: in Stephens's adaptation, Siobhan serves as the play's co-narrator — she reads aloud from Christopher's book while Christopher acts out the events, creating a play-within-a-play structure. This dual role (teacher in the story + narrator of the story) is unique to the play and central to AO2 analysis of dramatic form.
findings.source: National Theatre education resources on Christopher and Siobhan; Wikipedia (play article); SaveMyExams Eduqas GCSE notes; SparkNotes character analysis.

findings.location: Section: The A-Level Maths Exam and final paragraph
findings.claim: "The novel's final lines are characteristically understated. Christopher reflects: 'I know I can do this because I went to London on my own, and because I solved the mystery of Who Killed Wellington?... And that means I can do anything.'"
findings.issue: Two errors. (1) This presents the novel's ending as the text's ending, but Eduqas students study the play. The play ends differently: in the play, the final lines involve Christopher asking Siobhan a question — 'Does that mean I can do anything Siobhan?' — not making a declaration. This is a significant tonal shift (from declarative certainty to an open question) and an important difference in dramatic form. (2) The ellipsis between the quotes omits key lines from the full novel sentence: 'And I found my mother and I was brave and I wrote a book' — the omission changes the cumulative logic of Christopher's self-assessment. Teaching the truncated version risks students using an inexact quote in a closed-book exam.
findings.correction: Teach the play's ending: Christopher asks Siobhan 'Does that mean I can do anything Siobhan?' This question form reflects the play's more open, aspirational ending — Christopher's independence is emerging but uncertain. Also describe the post-show maths scene (unique to the play): after the curtain call, Christopher returns to solve his favourite A-level maths problem onstage with theatrical staging (music, lights, projections, confetti). If the novel ending is referenced for context, give the full untruncated quote.
findings.source: Play ending confirmed by multiple sources including a Quizlet of Siobhan's play lines; comparison of play vs novel endings in adaptation studies; LitCharts Chapter 233 for the full novel quote.

findings.location: Sections: Prime Number Chapters; Diagrams, Lists, and Mathematical Digressions; The Book-Within-a-Book
findings.claim: Lesson analyses the prime number chapter structure, diagrams, and mathematical inserts as features of 'the novel'. 'The novel includes diagrams, maps, timetables, mathematical proofs, logic puzzles, and lists.' 'The novel is framed as a book Christopher is writing.'
findings.issue: This lesson analyses structural and formal features that belong to the NOVEL, not to the Stephens play-text. The prime-numbered chapters do not exist in the play. The physical diagrams and mathematical inserts in the book's pages are not reproduced in the play — Stephens uses theatrical staging (projections, ensemble movement, lighting) to convey Christopher's mathematical and visual thinking. The book-within-a-book becomes a play-within-a-play in Stephens's version, with Siobhan reading aloud. Teaching these as features of 'the text' without specifying they are novel-only features will cause students to misattribute form analysis in the exam.
findings.correction: Restructure to clearly separate: (a) what Haddon does in the novel (prime chapters, physical diagrams, mathematical appendices, first-person prose narration), and (b) how Stephens translates these into theatrical form in the play (Siobhan's narration as the equivalent of first-person voice; projections/staging for the mathematical sequences; ensemble cast as a chorus representing Christopher's overwhelmed mind). The structural form of the play — two acts, Siobhan as narrator, ensemble staging — should be the core analysis, with the novel features as comparative context.
findings.source: Wikipedia (play article) on the play's adaptation strategies; National Theatre resources on adapting the novel; Conversation.com article 'The Curious Incident trades deadpan for high-octane' on theatrical choices.

findings.claim: "Christopher explicitly rejects metaphors: 'A metaphor is a lie. When I say the dog ran this is true. When you say the sky was crying this is a lie because the sky does not cry.'"
findings.issue: This is presented as a direct quotation, but the verified text from Chapter 29 of the novel reads: 'The word metaphor means carrying something from one place to another... it is when you describe something by using a word for something that it isn't... I think it should be called a lie because a pig is not like a day and people do not have skeletons in their cupboards.' The lesson's version uses different examples ('the dog ran'/'the sky was crying') which do not appear in the verified chapter-29 text. Presenting an unverified paraphrase as a direct quotation in a GCSE revision resource risks students memorising an inexact quote for closed-book exams.
findings.correction: Use verified phrasing from Chapter 29: Christopher explains that metaphors use a word for something it isn't, and says 'I think it should be called a lie because a pig is not like a day and people do not have skeletons in their cupboards.' Alternatively, clearly mark the 'sky crying' version as a paraphrase/illustration, not a direct quotation.
findings.source: Shmoop Chapter 29 quotes; SparkNotes Famous Quotes; multiple study guides quoting the 'pig is not like a day' example from Chapter 29.

findings.claim: "Writing in 2003, when autism was still widely pathologised, Haddon challenges the deficit model by presenting Christopher's logic and honesty as cognitive strengths that reveal truths neurotypical thinking obscures."
findings.issue: This AO4 context sentence attributes the text's choices to 'Haddon' and frames the work as a 2003 novel, but Eduqas students study the 2012 play by Simon Stephens. For AO4 (context), students should reference the play's context (2012 National Theatre premiere, Stephens's adaptation choices, the theatrical context of a play-within-a-play) alongside — or instead of — the novel's 2003 context. Attributing the exam-technique strategy to 'Haddon' when the exam requires analysis of 'Stephens' will lose marks.
findings.correction: Provide a play-framed AO4 context sentence, e.g.: 'Writing in 2012, adapting Haddon's novel for the stage, Stephens uses Siobhan's co-narration to present Christopher's perspective directly to the audience, challenging deficit-model attitudes toward autism by making Christopher's logic the lens through which the audience understands the world.' A second sentence could acknowledge the novel's 2003 context as the source material.
findings.source: Eduqas GCSE specification — students are examined on the Stephens play-text; AO4 requires context appropriate to the text studied.

findings.claim: "The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time was published in 2003 and became an immediate bestseller, winning the Whitbread Book of the Year."
findings.issue: Factually accurate for the novel but incomplete and misleading for the Eduqas context. (1) The lesson presents the work's context exclusively through the novel's publication and awards, with no mention of the play's 2012 premiere at the National Theatre, its Tony Award for Best Play, or its Olivier Award for Best Play. For a student studying the Stephens play, the theatrical context (National Theatre, 2012, Marianne Elliott's direction, the production's transfer to Broadway) is directly relevant to AO4. (2) The Whitbread award was specifically the Whitbread Novel Award and overall Whitbread Book of the Year 2003 — it is accurate, but without mentioning the play's awards, students are given an unbalanced picture of the text's cultural context.
findings.correction: Retain the novel's publication context (2003, Haddon, Whitbread) as background, then add the play's context: Simon Stephens adapted the novel for the stage; the play premiered at the National Theatre on 2 August 2012, directed by Marianne Elliott; it won both the Olivier Award for Best Play and the Tony Award for Best Play; the production transferred to Broadway in 2014. The play-within-a-play structure, Siobhan's narrator role, and the ensemble staging are Stephens's theatrical adaptations of Haddon's first-person novel format.
findings.source: Wikipedia (play article); National Theatre resources; Tony Awards database.

findings.claim: Ed confesses: "'I did it for you, Christopher. Because I didn't want you to know about your mum and Mr Shears.'"
findings.issue: This quote is presented as a direct speech quotation from Ed during his confession. It cannot be independently verified against the published play-script or novel as an exact verbatim quote. Multiple study resources describe the content of Ed's confession (he lied about Judy's death to protect Christopher from the pain of knowing she had left) but do not reproduce this specific wording. Teaching an unverified direct quotation as an exam-worthy quote risks students citing inaccurate wording in a closed-book exam.
findings.correction: Either verify this quote against the Methuen Drama GCSE Student Edition of the Stephens play-script, or present it as a paraphrase of Ed's confession rather than a direct quotation. The well-documented content of Ed's confession is: he lied about Judy dying because he thought it was better for Christopher than the truth of her abandonment; and he admits he killed Wellington in a rage after his relationship with Mrs Shears ended. Both facts are secure; the exact wording should be verified.
findings.source: Unable to verify exact wording from available sources; script verification against Methuen Drama edition recommended.

findings.location: Entire lesson — descriptions of 'the novel', Swindon vs London symbolism
findings.claim: Symbolism and setting analysis is written entirely in terms of the novel: 'Swindon represents Christopher's known world', 'The train journey from Swindon to London is the novel's central symbolic sequence.'
findings.issue: While the symbolic meanings of Swindon and London are valid for both novel and play, the lesson frames all analysis around 'the novel' and does not engage with how Stephens stages these settings theatrically. In the play, Swindon and London are not realistic sets — the National Theatre production used a bare stage with digital projections and ensemble movement to represent the overwhelming sensory experience of travel. The lesson's symbolism analysis would serve students better if it acknowledged how Stephens's staging choices (bare stage, projections, ensemble as crowd) create the contrast between familiar Swindon and overwhelming London. The 'train journey as symbol of independence' analysis is valid but should be framed around Stephens's theatrical choices, not 'the novel's central symbolic sequence'.
findings.correction: Retain the symbolic readings (Swindon = safety, London = chaos, train = independence) but add the play-specific layer: explain how Stephens stages these contrasts theatrically. Note that the play uses ensemble performers to embody the crowd and sensory overload that Christopher experiences on the journey — the ensemble cast physically enacts what the novel conveys through Christopher's narration.
findings.source: National Theatre production notes; multiple reviews of the original production describing the staging of the train journey.

findings.claim: "The final chapter includes Christopher's solution to a complex mathematical problem — presented in full — because for Christopher, mathematics is not a school subject but a language of certainty in an uncertain world."
findings.issue: The reference to 'the final chapter' again conflates novel and play. In the novel, the appendix contains a full mathematical proof. In the Stephens play, the maths problem is not an appendix — it is performed onstage in a post-curtain theatrical scene with music, lights, lasers, and confetti. The lesson's description of mathematics as 'presented in full' in 'the final chapter' is accurate only for the novel; for the play, the maths is staged as a live theatrical event after the main action ends. This distinction matters for AO2 (form, structure, theatrical technique).
findings.correction: Distinguish novel and play: in the novel, Haddon includes a printed mathematical appendix. In Stephens's play, the maths problem is staged theatrically after the curtain call — Christopher returns to solve his 'favourite question' from the A-level paper while the stage uses projections, music, and lighting. This theatrical staging transforms the novel's printed appendix into a live performance of mathematical thinking, which is a significant choice about theatrical form.
findings.source: Multiple sources on the play's epilogue maths scene, including WJEC official resource PDF and Seneca Learning notes on the maths appendix.

findings.location: Section: Christopher's World: Rules and Routines
findings.claim: "4 red cars in a row meant it was a Good Day. 4 yellow cars in a row meant it was a Black Day."
findings.issue: The colour/car system Christopher uses is verified as a feature of the novel. In the novel, it is described in Christopher's first-person narration. In the Stephens play, this detail is communicated through Siobhan's reading of Christopher's book/narration rather than via Christopher describing it directly to the audience. The lesson presents this as though Christopher narrates it in first person ('Haddon presents these rules not as quirks but as Christopher's way of imposing order') — attributing the choice to Haddon. For the play, Stephens uses Siobhan's reading of this passage to establish Christopher's rules, which has a different dramatic effect. The fact is correct; the attribution to 'Haddon' and 'the novel' is the issue.
findings.correction: Note that in the play, this detail is conveyed through Siobhan's narration (she reads from Christopher's book), not through Christopher speaking directly to the audience — a different relationship between character and audience than in the novel's first-person narration.
findings.source: Play adaptation structure confirmed by National Theatre resources and Wikipedia (play article).

findings.claim: "The novel we read is presented as the book Christopher is writing... This metafictional device... creates a double perspective: we read Christopher's book while also reading Haddon's novel."
findings.issue: The metafictional analysis is correct for the novel but needs adaptation for the play. In the play, the book-within-a-book becomes a play-within-a-play: Siobhan reads from Christopher's book while Christopher acts out events onstage. The 'double perspective' in the play is between Siobhan as narrator (reading/interpreting) and Christopher as actor (enacting) — which is a different theatrical mechanism from reading a novel. The lesson describes the novel's device but does not explain how Stephens translates it into theatrical form.
findings.correction: Add the play-specific translation: Stephens converts Haddon's book-within-a-book into a play-within-a-play by giving Siobhan the narration. The double perspective in the play is between what Siobhan reads (Christopher's written account) and what the audience sees Christopher doing onstage — the gap between these two creates the same interpretive effect as the novel's ironic gap between narrator and story.
findings.source: National Theatre resources on the adaptation; Wikipedia (play article); SaveMyExams Eduqas GCSE plot and context notes.

findings.claim: Key quotations listed: 'I do not tell lies'; 'that is not your fault'; 'I can do anything'; 'I find people confusing.'
findings.issue: Three of these four quotations are accurate novel quotations. 'I can do anything' is problematic for Eduqas students. In the play, Christopher does not make this declarative statement — he asks Siobhan 'Does that mean I can do anything Siobhan?' The declarative form ('I can do anything') is a novel quote, not a play quote. Teaching it as a key quotation to memorise for the Eduqas play exam means students will learn incorrect wording. The other three quotations ('I do not tell lies', 'that is not your fault', 'I find people confusing') are widely attested across both novel and play.
findings.correction: For the Eduqas play exam, the equivalent of the novel's 'I can do anything' is the play's 'Does that mean I can do anything Siobhan?' — a question to Siobhan, not a statement. The distinction matters both for accuracy and for AO2 analysis: the question form in the play creates a more open, uncertain ending than the novel's declarative confidence.
findings.source: Play ending confirmed by multiple adaptation sources; Quizlet of Siobhan's play lines; contrast with Chapter 233 novel ending in SparkNotes and LitCharts.

findings.claim: "Christopher discovers that Mr Shears (Mrs Shears's ex-husband) used to be a friend of his parents, and that Mr Shears and Christopher's mother used to spend time together."
findings.issue: Accurate but incomplete. The full facts confirmed by multiple sources: Roger Shears (Mr Shears) is Mrs Shears's ex-husband who had an affair with Judy Boone (Christopher's mother) and went to live with her in London. Mrs Alexander (the elderly neighbour) is the one who tells Christopher that Mr Shears and his mother had an affair — this is a specific character action that demonstrates Mrs Alexander's role and should be attributed correctly.
findings.correction: Clarify: it is Mrs Alexander who informs Christopher that his mother and Mr Shears had an affair. This is one of Mrs Alexander's key contributions to the plot and a demonstration of the adults' web of hidden relationships that Christopher gradually uncovers.
findings.source: SparkNotes Character Analysis — Mrs Alexander; LitCharts Mrs Alexander character page; GradeSaver Q&A.

summary.overarching_issue: The entire 8-lesson unit has been written as analysis of Haddon's 2003 NOVEL, but Eduqas GCSE teaches the Simon Stephens 2012 PLAY. This is a fundamental medium error that runs through all 8 lessons. Students taught from these lessons will misidentify the text, misattribute craft choices, reference novel-specific structural devices (prime-numbered chapters, printed mathematical appendices) that do not exist in the play-text, and may give the wrong final quotation in the exam.
most_critical: CI-001: All 8 lessons analyse 'the novel' by 'Haddon' — Eduqas students study the Stephens PLAY. All craft attribution should reference 'Stephens' and the play-text.
CI-002: Lessons 2, 3, 4 are organised by chapter numbers (novel feature only). The play has acts/scenes, not chapters.
CI-003: Siobhan's role as co-narrator (the play's defining structural device) is absent from the Character Analysis lesson. She is incorrectly called a 'teaching assistant'.

CI-004: Final quotation given as the novel's declarative 'I can do anything'. The play ends with Christopher asking Siobhan a question: 'Does that mean I can do anything Siobhan?' — a fundamentally different tone and form.

CI-005: The Structure lesson analyses prime-numbered chapters and physical diagrams/appendices as features of 'the text' — these are novel-only devices. Stephens uses theatrical staging, projections, and Siobhan's narration instead.
what_is_correct: Core plot facts are accurate: Wellington's death by garden fork, letters from Judy, Ed's confession (both Wellington and the lie about Judy), the journey to London, the A-level maths A*, Sandy the golden retriever puppy, Christopher's logical thinking as both strength and limitation.

Character relationships are accurate: Ed's love alongside his lies, Judy's exhaustion and return, Siobhan's supportive role, Mr Shears's affair with Judy, Mrs Alexander's role in revealing the affair.
Themes analysis (truth/lies, family, neurodiversity, bravery, independence) is thematically sound.
The Sherlock Holmes / Silver Blaze title reference is correctly identified.
Wellington is correctly described as Mrs Shears's dog killed by Ed with a garden fork.
Sandy is correctly identified as a golden retriever puppy given to Christopher by Ed.
The Whitbread Book of the Year claim for the novel is accurate.
Judy's letter quote ('I am not a very good mother... that is not your fault') is authentic.
The prime numbers explanation and quote ('what is left when you have taken all the patterns away') are accurate for the novel.
summary.recommended_action: Full rewrite of all 8 lessons to reframe around the Stephens play-text: update all 'the novel'/'Haddon presents' references to 'the play'/'Stephens'; replace chapter-based lesson titles with act/scene-based organisation; add Siobhan's co-narrator role as a central theatrical device throughout; correct the final quotation to the play's version; add the post-curtain maths scene as a distinctive play feature; update AO4 context to foreground the 2012 National Theatre premiere and Tony/Olivier wins.
